implementation_notes: C++ has no library lazy value of its own: the stand-in is a hand-written class that implements the same interface and guards a std::unique_ptr with std::call_once, so the real subject is built once on first use and reused afterwards. The guard itself is not hand-rolled - std::call_once with std::once_flag guarantees exactly-once execution, and function-local static initialization gives the same guarantee for a fixed subject; std::call_once treats a throwing initializer as exceptional and retries on the next call, which is the hook for retry policy. Prefer this shape when the proxy must own a polymorphic subject built from runtime arguments; std::optional in-place storage (C++17) drops the allocation when the type is known statically.
pitfalls: Unique ownership makes the proxy non-copyable; a copy that re-initializes creates a second expensive subject, so share through a shared_ptr or make the type non-copyable explicitly.
The initializer runs while std::call_once serializes callers, so a slow construction blocks other accessors and a reentrant construction deadlocks.
If the initializer throws, the flag is not flipped and the build is retried on the next call; inside a destructor or a noexcept path that retry can terminate the program.

variants.name: Proxy with in-place std::optional storage
variants.implementation_notes: When the subject type is known statically, hold it by value in a std::optional inside the proxy and build it with emplace() on first access, still behind a std::call_once or an atomic guard; std::optional manages a value that may or may not be present, and the nested object's lifetime starts at emplace(), so no heap allocation or pointer indirection is needed. Choose it for expensive-but-allocatable subjects (parsers, decoded buffers, large structs) where the extra storage in every unused stand-in is cheaper than an allocation, and note that std::optional's storage exists for the whole lifetime of the stand-in even when the value was never constructed.
pitfalls: The optional reserves raw storage for the subject in every stand-in, so a large subject inflates each unused proxy even when it is never built.
emplace() on an engaged optional destroys and rebuilds the value; only the guard may call it, and reset() silently sends the next access back through the initializer.
Dereferencing the optional outside the guard is undefined behaviour while it is disengaged, so the accessor must be the only entry point.
